Intel's Cheapest Arc G3 Handheld Chip Reportedly Called "Arc G3 Play"

by
DrUsmanSaleem
 Today, 18:25 Discuss (2 Comments)
Videocardz reports that Intel is working on a new Arc G3 handheld chip, called Arc G3 Play, for affordable handhelds. The report says that this part will slot in below the Arc G3 and G3 Extreme, and will have just four Xe3 GPU cores. The Arc G3 has 10 Xe3 cores, while the top-end Xe3 Extreme has 12. This new chip will sit below both existing SKUs and target cheaper handhelds. The CPU configuration is not well-known currently, but an earlier leak from August points to four P-cores and four LPE cores in a 4+0+4+4 configuration. Leaker Jaykihn later changed that claim, suggesting a 0+8+0+4 configuration instead. The Videocardz report considers the latter more likely, although this question seems open right now.

As far as the Arc G3 SoC, its appeal is mostly centered around price. Current Arc G3 handhelds aren't exactly cheap, with the GPD Win Mini Ultra we recently covered starting at $1,699. That particular model uses an Arc G3 Extreme SoC. We can make an educated guess that Intel may be targeting the sub-$1000 market with this new SKU. The Arc G3 Play will only have 4 Xe3 cores, so its reasonable to expect modest performance out of it that won't top any benchmark charts. Handhelds sporting this particular chip should be fine for lighter titles at lower resolutions, and may be helped by Intel XeSS quite a bit. We still don't know the clock speeds, memory support, target handhelds, and there's even conflicting rumors about the power envelope. More information about the Arc G3 Play should surface in the coming weeks.

Intel Lands an Unnamed External Customer for Its 18A-P Node

by
DrUsmanSaleem
 Today, 16:31 Discuss (9 Comments)
Intel CEO Lip-Bu Tan says the company has signed its first outside customer for 18A, although he kept the customer anonymous. It was first reported by CNBC that Tan mentioned the Intel 18A node while speaking at the TomorrowX Summit in Austin last Wednesday, but Intel CTO Pushkar Ranade later confirmed on X that the deal was for 18A-P specifically. That node entered risk production in June, and Intel claims it offers 9% higher performance at the same power, or 18% lower power at the same performance, compared to 18A. This deal is for the first external customer, but Intel is using the 18A-P node internally. For instance, Lip-Bu Tan has confirmed that the upcoming Nova Lake CPU lineup is set to use Intel 18A-P as well. That node is also design-rule compatible with 18A, so existing designs should carry over without requiring any major rework.

Of course, the specifics are quite limited at this point. Intel hasn't shared which customer it is, what volumes are being discussed, or a production timeline for when we can expect external products on this node. There are also some conflicting reports about the "first" label, since Socionext said back in August that it would use the 18A-P node for its custom SoCs. However, it's possible that this is the first signed manufacturing deal, and the specifics of the Socionext contract were a bit different. On the same day, Microsoft confirmed it will use Intel's EMIB packaging for its Azure chips and also secured multi-year Xeon supply. That will most likely include the new "Diamond Rapids" platform as well. Attendees also quoted Tan as saying 18A yields are now at 70%, but those reports are unconfirmed for now. It looks like Intel Foundry is slowly gaining momentum, but a lot of questions still remain, including about Intel's next-gen 14A node.

Microsoft Patent Filing Targets Easier Thumbstick Swaps

by
DrUsmanSaleem
 Today, 15:42 Discuss (4 Comments)
We all know how annoying and fragile thumbsticks can be sometimes. Everyone has experienced the dreaded stick drift at least once in their gaming career, but the most frustrating part is that there is no easy way to repair it. However, it looks like Microsoft may be working on a solution behind the scenes. A Microsoft patent application titled "Replaceable Input Module," spotted by Patentlyze, describes a self-contained stick module that drops right into the controller and locks down with a single screw. That could mean, in theory, fixing a broken thumbstick would take only a screwdriver and a few minutes of time. Looking into the patent, the screw seemingly stays attached to the module, so you can't easily lose it either. There's a locating pin and an angled lip line to line it up, with contacts on the underside of the module that replace a soldered connection.

The patent also mentions redundant contacts in case one gets dirty. Moreover, there's an ID signal that tells the controller which module is currently installed. The company names keyboards, laptops, and drone controllers as possible uses in addition to gamepads, but the design isn't currently linked to any product officially. The application was filed on May 8, 2025, and was published on November 12, but it was rejected in the examiner's first review. That's pretty common in the patent world, and usually only means amended claims. It's important to remember that this is just a patent, but if it were to turn into a real product, that would make Xbox controllers a lot more repairable. Currently, thumbsticks on Xbox controllers are soldered to the board, and stick drift often means you have to replace the whole pad. There's no word yet on whether this technology will show up in Xbox Project Helix controllers.

Phison Previews an SSD That Runs AI Frameworks on Its Own NPU

by
DrUsmanSaleem
 Today, 01:23 Discuss (5 Comments)
Everyone's going all in on AI, so SSD manufacturers were not going to be left behind. Phison has detailed an enterprise SSD design that can run AI frameworks on the drive itself. At the Supercomputing 2026 (SC26) event in Chicago, the company showed off the computational storage design that hosts both an NPU and 64 GB of onboard memory running at 130 GB/s. It also supports PyTorch, vLLM, OpenVINO, and llama.ccp. Phison says this SSD could cut data transfers by 10 to 100 times for suitable workloads. It achieves that by scanning and processing the dataset in parallel, so it only sends back the relevant results instead of moving the entire dataset over the host. The company uses DMIPS to rate its NPU performance instead of using TOPS, which is a bit unusual.

Phison has shown off other AI-focused storage projects before, and this SSD is the latest one in that chain. At the same event, Phison showcased a Mixed media design that removes the need for dedicated cache drives by putting high-endurance pSLC and QLC flash behind a single 16-channel controller. Phison says that losing one drive in a 24-drive server would cost only 4% of the cache instead of the usual 25%. Its showcase also included the PCIe Gen 6 X3 controller that was first shown at Computex. As for the SSD with the built-in NPU, it is sparse on details for now. We don't know what kind of controller, interface, form factor, or memory type it uses or plans to use. These are products that are still in development, so it's best to treat them as proof of concepts for now.

Intel Nova Lake-H Spec Sheet Shows Up With a 4.8 GHz Boost and 25 W TDP

by
DrUsmanSaleem
 Yesterday, 23:58 Discuss (1 Comment)
As we move closer to Nova Lake's eventual launch, more and more details are surfacing about the various lineups under that umbrella. We covered the sighting of the 28-core Intel "Nova Lake-S" desktop CPU on Openbenchmark today, and now we have an early look at the Nova Lake-H lineup. Advantech's preliminary datasheet for the ASR-A505 model gives us a glance at the Core Ultra Series 4 "Nova Lake-H" laptop silicon. This is a 4-inch single-board computer built for autonomous mobile robots. The 16-core chip on this board is listed with a 4.8 GHz boost clock, a 2.0 GHz P-core base clock, 18 MB of last-level cache, and a 25 W TDP. The last bit might be configurable between 15-25 W, according to the block diagram.

There's also a spec readout that's quite confusing. Advantech lists the chip as an "8P+4E+4LE" part, which doesn't match any SKU that has leaked so far. According to leaker Jaykihn's earlier posts, the lineup's 16-core model was an Ultra 9 4970H with a 4P+8E+4LPE configuration. This was also corroborated by leaker momomo_us and a Nova Lake-H package photo that showed the same 4+8+4 arrangement. However, it's quite possible that this is a typo and Advantech accidentally swapped the P-core and E-core counts, as this is a preliminary document.

Moore Threads Claims Its Next GPU Will Break the Consumer VRAM Record

by
DrUsmanSaleem
 Yesterday, 20:56 Discuss (19 Comments)
Another player is coming to stake their claim against NVIDIA, AMD, and Intel in the GPU market. A product manager behind Moore Threads' MTT S80 claims that the company's next desktop graphics card, codenamed Lushan, could set the record for the largest VRAM capacity ever put on a consumer graphics card. He posted this on November 18 on Weibo, but didn't disclose how much VRAM it would actually have. After that, Moore Threads published its first poster for MDC 2026, and the artwork hints at the graphics card. It is mostly hidden behind a pair of peaks, with one rendered as a 3D mesh and the other as a neural network. MDC is the MUSA Developer Conference, set for December 29 in Beijing.

We saw the concept behind Lushan at the first MUSA Developer Conference last December, alongside the Huagang architecture. The company then claimed 15x higher AAA gaming performance than its previous generation, as well as 50x faster ray tracing and 64x more compute, some truly gigantic leaps. If we look at what Moore Threads is claiming, the target to beat is the GeForce RTX 5090 at 32 GB of VRAM (if you consider the 5090 a consumer card at all). The MTT S80 has 16 GB of VRAM, and Moore Threads has previously promised four times the memory capacity over its predecessor. That works out to 64 GB, which would definitely be a record, but this is speculation, and Moore Threads has not confirmed any number at the time of writing. There's also debate over whether gamers really need that much VRAM, and whether such a large memory pool would attract workstation and local LLM users instead.

SilverStone Equips HELA 1350Rz With Three EPS Cables, Citing Nova Lake-S "High Power Demands"

by
DrUsmanSaleem
 Yesterday, 20:27 Discuss (7 Comments)
SilverStone has published the product page for the HELA 1350Rz on its website, which is a 1350 W, ATX 3.1 PSU with 80 Plus Platinum certification. It is a fully modular PSU, but the interesting bit is that it ships with three 4+4-pin EPS cables, whereas PSU units in this class usually come with two. SilverStone's reasoning is that the extra cable is there for the "high power demands of Intel NVL-S CPUs," referring of course to Intel's upcoming Core Ultra 4000 "Nova Lake-S" desktop CPUs. Graphics cards don't get that special treatment, as the unit carries the usual two native 12V-2x6 connectors. As for the PSU itself, it measures 150 x 86 x 160 mm and reportedly uses Japanese capacitors along with a 135 mm fluid dynamic bearing fan.

This "extra cable" lines up nicely with leaks from earlier this year, particularly about the 52-core NVL-S variant that has been at the center of rumors for a while. Prominent Intel leaker Jaykihn backed a report that Intel's 52-core Nova Lake-S flagship, the one with a dual compute tile design, carries a staggering 474 W PL2. Moreover, Intel's Z990 reference design allows for three 8-pin EPS connectors as well. Therefore, it looks like the third EPS cable is there to provide the additional power for the flagship 52-core Nova Lake-S variant, if needed. Jaykihn also claimed that the three connectors on Z990 boards are "nice to have" vendor options and don't unlock a higher power state. It would be reasonable to assume that the 52-core variant would perform adequately on just two EPS connectors as well, but the extra one would come in handy while overclocking.

Sony's Patented Collar Would Blow Air on Players, Likely During VR Games

by
DrUsmanSaleem
 Yesterday, 19:29 Discuss (16 Comments)
If you're familiar with Sony's patents, you know they can be quite ambitious sometimes. Continuing that trend, Sony Interactive Entertainment recently filed a patent application for a curved neckband with air vents on the inner side that would blow air towards the wearer's neck, chin, and face. The filing (US 2026/0357800 A1), spotted by Patentlyze, went public on November 12. Sony itself describes the goal as a way to "increase the sense of immersion." Apparently, there is also a built-in communication unit that takes control signals from an external device and decides which vents fire and how hard. That external device would likely be a console or a PC.

Looking at the design, the filing shows eight tiny blowers spaced around the collar that would act as the outlets for air. Sony also mentions piezoelectric elements that vibrate a thin plate at high speed, apparently so the airflow can keep up with what happens on screen. Some of the diagrams are quite interesting too, including one where an enemy is approaching from the back, and the collar is supposed to alert the player to their existence. Apparently, some stimuli can trigger more frequent and stronger puffs of air, and there is also mention of wind effects for racing games. A schematic pairs the neckband with a VR headset, so maybe the PS VR2 or its successor is the target for this technology. Of course, a patent is not a finished product, and companies (especially Sony) file lots of them that go nowhere. Here's a similar one about turning game audio into visual cues for hearing-impaired players.

28-Core Intel "Nova Lake-S" Appears in Testing Running at 5.2 GHz

by
AleksandarK
 Yesterday, 15:39 Discuss (55 Comments)
Intel's single-compute die "Nova Lake-S" variant has been spotted with a 28-core configuration and a boost frequency of 5.2 GHz, according to the OpenBenchmark testing suite. During the tests, a processor named Intel 0000 appeared with the "NVL" identifier, suggesting that a "Nova Lake-S" SKU with this configuration is indeed present. The processor's identification as Intel 0000 implies that the rumored four-number naming scheme is real, as confirmed by the benchmarks. This naming scheme could easily become standard, moving away from the three-digit SKU naming we've seen in the past.

Interestingly, the submission also identifies the integrated graphics as Intel NVL-S, indicating that the engineering platform is being tested beyond just CPU workloads. The tests include various graphics and compute applications, such as Quake II RTX, Unigine benchmarks, Hashcat, and multiple OpenCL workloads. While the 5.2 GHz figure is promising, it should not be taken as confirmation of the processor's final boost frequency. Engineering samples can operate with different firmware, power limits, and clock configurations than retail products. The listing also does not disclose whether the reported frequency represents a sustained operating clock or a maximum observed value.

LG's 1000 Hz UltraGear Uses a TCL CSOT Panel, Inkjet OLED Monitors Could Follow

by
DrUsmanSaleem
 Yesterday, 00:31 Discuss (14 Comments)
At the DTC 2026 conference in Wuhan, China, CSOT CEO Jun Zhao confirmed that the 1000 Hz panel inside LG's UltraGear 25G590B comes from TCL CSOT. Zhao said that the company supplies a 24.5-inch FHD LCD panel with IPS technology for that monitor. Apparently, this is the first time CSOT has mass-produced a 1000 Hz LCD. These panels reportedly come from its Gen 8.5 T9 LCD fab in Guangzhou. It's interesting that LG chose TCL CSOT for the UltraGear 25G590B panel, considering the IPS LCD market has mostly been led by BOE and LG Display, the latter being LG Electronics' own display arm. CSOT also produces IPS panels at its T10 fab, which it bought from LG Display, so there's some prior connection there.

There's more to come from this collaboration, apparently. An LG Electronics official said at the event that the company is considering 5K and 6K inkjet-printed OLED panels for its monitors, planned for around 2028 or 2029. Inkjet printing is a technique in which the OLED material is deposited through nozzles instead of being evaporated through a fine metal mask. We previously reported that TCL CSOT is planning inkjet-printed OLED panels up to 700 Hz for 2028 or 2029. To support this, CSOT's larger Gen 8.6 T8 Inkjet OLED line in Guangzhou is now installing equipment. LG is currently evaluating this idea, so it's not a done deal at the time of writing. However, Zhao says T8 remains on track for mass production in Q4 2027.

NVIDIA's SSD Write Bug Gets Patched in GeForce Hotfix 621.35 Driver

by
DrUsmanSaleem

NVIDIA today has released the GeForce Hotfix 621.35 driver to fix the bug that was hammering SSDs while idle. There is only one fix in the release: "Excessive writes to file nvlog.nvlgstg may occur in the background," and that was all that was needed on an urgent basis. We reported the issue of constant and excessive SSD writes that was spotted by several NVIDIA users earlier this week, particularly on drivers 621.14 and 621.24. The association expects the PCB shortage to last through at least the first half of 2027, and meaningful relief is unlikely before mid-2028.

Microsoft is finally enabling Remote Direct Memory Access (RDMA) over the USB4 protocol on Windows 11, allowing multiple PCs to be daisy-chained and used together to process large workloads. This means that Windows 11 now has a mechanism to distribute a workload across multiple interconnected PCs, enabling faster processing. Essentially, AI inferencing at home is now limited by the number of PCs and their specifications, rather than a single PC. RDMA allows the workload to directly access system memory on another PC, all through USB4, which offers up to 80 Gbps bandwidth for fast data transfer.

Instead of using Ethernet over USB4 in a UDP packet configuration, Microsoft chose to implement RDMA over USB4 to significantly reduce data access latency. Microsoft interconnected two PCs to measure round-trip latency by message size, finding that RDMA over USB4 achieves latency between 28 and 50 microseconds. In contrast, Ethernet over USB4 using UDP results in latency between 116 and 194 microseconds, making the RDMA implementation roughly four times faster. This lower latency will greatly benefit systems running large workloads, especially in latency-sensitive tasks like AI inferencing. A 512 Gb wafer now goes for about $14.30, which is 32% below last quarter, and 1 Tb products are down 19% to $24.90. Apparently, the reasoning is weak consumer demand, since buyers are now delaying upgrades due to high prices. Moreover, phone manufacturers are trimming base storage specs, and PC makers are selling through their existing stock as shipments continue to fall.

That's the spot side of the story, but contract prices run on long-term deals and have been slower to react. Bank of America reportedly expects smartphone and PC NAND contract prices to fall 5-10% QoQ in Q1 2027, while enterprise products are expected to hold flat or slightly creep up. TrendForce also expects overall NAND contract prices to slip 0-5% in Q2 2027. In light of all these predictions, it looks like there is some relief on the horizon as far as NAND prices go. That's a turnaround from early reports that predicted the shortage would last at least three more years. However, now it looks like SSD prices will continue to fall slowly but surely into 2027, at least on the consumer side.

AGESA isn't publicly available software, it is a software component that's encapsulated into system firmware by OEMs, and implementing it requires an OEM to be doing business with AMD and be subject to its terms of sale and other agreements. However, for the desktop "Zen 6" Ryzen family, codenamed "Olympic Ridge," AMD is switching to TSMC's N2X node, an enhanced variant of the standard N2 that targets higher frequencies. This switch results in delayed mass production and rollout of desktop Ryzen. TSMC plans to begin mass production of its N2X node in 2027, meaning "Olympic Ridge" will likely arrive a few months later, with Computex 2027 being the probable announcement date.

AMD likely chose the N2X node for its higher clock potential. Originally, TSMC targeted HPC workloads, but desktop processors can also benefit from high clock speeds for maximum performance. The N2X node offers two advantages over the standard N2: an ultra-high performance standard cell that delivers a 5% higher clock speed, and a high-speed device, which provides an additional 5% boost, resulting in a combined 10% speed increase.
